1.title: Life Cycles, Agile, Hybrid and Tailoring
1.text: Welcome to Module 2. About sixty percent of the items on the exam involve agile or hybrid situations, and almost every scenario asks you to know which approach is in play. This module gives you the toolkit. In Part 1, we look at life cycles and the three development approaches: predictive, adaptive and hybrid. Part 2 goes inside agile and hybrid ways of working. Part 3 teaches tailoring.

1.title: Where This Module Sits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits. In the Process domain, Task 1 asks you to develop the integrated plan and plan delivery. That includes assessing needs and complexity, and recommending a predictive, agile or hybrid approach. Beyond that single task, the split runs across all three domains: about forty percent of items are predictive, and about sixty percent are agile, adaptive or hybrid. So you must be comfortable in both worlds. The same problem often has a different best answer in each.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do six things. Describe phases, gates and the project life cycle, and explain how risk and the cost of change evolve. Compare predictive, adaptive and hybrid approaches, and choose among them. Tell iterative from incremental delivery, and pick a delivery cadence. Use backlogs, iterations, flow and agile measures. Explain hybrid practice, including planning, reporting, change control and metrics. And tailor processes, the approach and engagement, and diagnose common problems.

1.title: Case Check-In: A Hybrid Project
1.text: Our running case is a hybrid project. The physical build follows a predictive approach: permits, procurement, construction and commissioning, with phase gates and formal change control. The controller software and the dashboard follow an agile approach, in two-week iterations with a product owner. The two lanes meet at integration points, such as the controller interface and commissioning. Throughout this module, ask which lane a problem sits in, because the best answer depends on it.

1.title: Key Terms
1.text: Six terms to fix. The project life cycle is the series of phases a project passes through. A phase is a set of related activities ending in a deliverable, and a phase gate is the review held before the next phase. The development approach is how the product is created and evolved: predictive, adaptive or hybrid. A timebox is a fixed period, often one to four weeks. Iterative work refines through repeated cycles, while incremental work delivers usable pieces. And delivery cadence is how often outcomes are delivered.

1.title: Phases and Gates
1.text: Phases have attributes. A phase can carry a name, a number, a duration, resource needs, entry criteria and exit criteria. Exit criteria may tie to acceptance criteria, contractual obligations or performance targets. Entry criteria may check resource availability, verified viability and alignment with organizational goals. Gates normally sit at the end of a phase, but they can also sit at the start, to check alignment, resources and risks before work begins. Organizations often standardize a few life cycles. If none is prescribed, the team picks the best one.

1.title: What a Phase Gate Decides
1.text: A phase gate compares performance and progress with the project and business documents, and leads to a decision. Often called a go or no-go, it has more than two outcomes. Continue to the next phase. Continue with modification. End the project or phase. Remain in the phase. Repeat the phase or parts of it. Or park the project temporarily, for example for an urgent initiative. So when exit criteria are not met, the best answer reports the facts and lets the gate authority decide. It never records them as met.

1.title: How Variables Change Over Time
1.text: Look at how variables change over a predictive project. Cost and staffing start low, rise during the work, and drop rapidly at the end. Risk and uncertainty are greatest at the start and fall as decisions are made and deliverables are accepted. Stakeholders have the most influence on change at the start, when changes can raise value without large cost or schedule impact. That influence falls while the cost of change rises. In adaptive work, stakeholders take part throughout, so risks surface earlier through consistent feedback.

1.title: The Spectrum of Approaches
1.text: Approaches form a spectrum. Predictive sits at one end, adaptive at the other, and hybrid in between. The project manager and the team choose from the project's characteristics. Requirements, scope, timeline and goals. Organizational culture and stakeholder involvement. Risk, technology and complexity. Clear and stable requirements, heavy regulation, costly change and a fixed date favor predictive. Uncertain requirements, valuable early feedback and small self-managed teams favor adaptive. Mixed situations favor hybrid, and most modern projects are mixed.

1.title: Predictive Approaches
1.text: Predictive approaches are also called waterfall, plan-driven or traditional. They are best when scope can be stabilized early, and requirements, cost and risks can be defined well. Much of the planning is done up front, and you need robust change control. They suit situations where iterating costs far more than it gives, such as the build phase of construction, and heavily regulated fields such as healthcare. A predictive project can still deliver in increments, with scope largely fixed. A typical flow is feasibility, design, build, check, transfer and close.

1.title: Adaptive Approaches
1.text: Adaptive approaches are also called change-driven or agile. They are best when requirements and technical solutions are highly uncertain and likely to change. You set a clear vision at the start, and requirements are progressively elaborated with feedback. Iterations of one to four weeks end with a demonstration, and the whole team selects work from a prioritized backlog. Flow-based scheduling optimizes the flow of work and comes from Kanban and the theory of constraints. And agile is a mindset, broader than any single framework.

1.title: Four Delivery Styles
1.text: Four delivery styles. Single delivery plans and builds everything, then delivers at the end. Incremental delivery gives usable pieces, each building on the last, so value arrives earlier. Iterative delivery refines the same product through repeated cycles, from rough to polished, using feedback. Agile is both iterative and incremental, with short timeboxes, a demonstration, feedback and a reprioritized backlog each time. Here is an example. A team releases a payment module in month two and reporting in month four, with the full scope planned at the start. That is incremental delivery inside a predictive project.

1.title: Fixed and Variable Constraints
1.text: Think of constraints as fixed or variable. When scope is fixed, unexpected changes are absorbed by changing the schedule or the budget. That is typical of predictive work. When schedule and budget are fixed, unexpected changes are absorbed by varying scope. That is typical of timeboxed agile work. So when an agile team has a fixed budget and date and new priorities keep arriving, reprioritize the backlog so that the highest-value items fit. Do not promise all the scope.

1.title: Hybrid Approaches: Four Patterns
1.text: Hybrid combines adaptive and predictive elements. PMBOK 8 notes that most modern projects benefit from it: flexibility to adapt, with control over predictable aspects. Four patterns are common. Adaptive early, then a predictive rollout, like designing a custom home iteratively and then building once. Both at the same time, such as software built adaptively while a data center is built predictively. Mainly predictive with one small adaptive part. And mainly adaptive with one fixed component, such as a regulatory approval.

1.title: Hybrid Levels
1.text: Disciplined Agile describes three hybrid levels. At level one, predictive dominates, and some adaptive elements reduce pain points. At level two, both approaches contribute significantly. At level three, adaptive dominates, and some predictive elements satisfy business constraints. Suppose a bank must follow a mandatory release process with fixed change windows and audit sign-offs, but the team adds short feedback loops to cut rework. Predictive leads there, with adaptive elements added. That is level one.

1.title: Choosing the Approach: Deliverable Factors
1.text: Selection factors come in three groups. First, the deliverables. High innovation pushes toward adaptive. Certain, easy-to-define requirements push toward predictive. Less stable scope pushes toward adaptive. When change is difficult or costly, predictive fits. If the deliverable can be delivered in components, adaptive or hybrid fits. Rigorous safety rules and heavy regulation point to predictive. And significant value from frequent user feedback points to adaptive. Remember that different deliverables in one project may use different approaches.

1.title: Choosing the Approach: Project and Organization Factors
1.text: The next two groups are project and organization factors. Stakeholders who can be deeply involved favor adaptive. For schedule, value in early partial delivery favors adaptive, while a fixed end date favors predictive. Uncertain financing favors adaptive and iterative work. Large, complex and evolving work needs flexible approaches. Experienced, collaborative teams favor adaptive. Structure and culture matter: hierarchical organizations lean predictive, and networked, self-managed ones lean adaptive or hybrid. Adaptive teams are often three to nine people. A hierarchical organization adopting agile should align policies and reporting, or go step by step.

1.title: Delivery Cadence
1.text: Delivery cadence describes how often outcomes are delivered. Single delivery: everything at the end. Multiple deliveries: components at different times, in sequence or in parallel, like building security upgrades in stages. Periodic deliveries: multiple deliveries on a regular, fixed schedule, common in adaptive work, such as internal releases every two weeks. Continuous delivery: incrementally delivering value to production on an ongoing basis, with the product always production-ready. In every case, deliveries must meet or exceed the target business objectives.

1.title: The Five Focus Areas
1.text: The five Focus Areas are the fundamental actions of any project, whatever the approach. Initiating authorizes the project and aligns expectations. Planning establishes scope and objectives, and it is progressive: iterative or rolling wave, with continual refinement. Executing does the work, and the plan can and should change whenever the change adds value. Monitoring and controlling compares actual with planned, analyzes variance and recommends corrective action, running in parallel. Closing verifies outputs, outcomes and benefits and transitions to operations. They are not phases. In an adaptive project, every iteration contains planning, executing and monitoring and controlling.

1.title: Life Cycle Traps: What PMI Expects
1.text: The traps for Part 1. Match the approach to the context, not to your preference. Hybrid is a legitimate, often best answer for mixed scenarios. Incremental is not iterative. Focus Areas are not phases, so planning continues as the plan is refined. Phase gates are decision points, not rubber stamps. In fixed-budget, fixed-date agile work, scope flexes. And closing verifies outcomes and benefits, not just the handover. Finally, the plan may change when the change adds value. Use the change process, and do not follow the baseline rigidly.

1.title: Part 1 Recap
1.text: Let us recap Part 1. A life cycle has phases with entry and exit criteria, and a gate decides among six outcomes. Predictive, adaptive and hybrid approaches are chosen by context. Delivery can be single, incremental, iterative or agile, with a cadence from single to continuous. When scope is fixed, time and cost flex. When time and cost are fixed, scope flexes. Hybrid has four patterns and three levels. And Focus Areas are not phases, so planning and control continue throughout.

2.title: Agile: Mindset and Roles
2.text: Part 2 goes inside agile and hybrid ways of working. Agile is a mindset of values and principles, broader than any framework. Agile approaches are adaptive: you set a vision first, and requirements are elaborated by feedback. Servant leadership means leading by understanding and addressing the needs and development of team members, in service of the project's business objectives. Iterations last one to four weeks, and teams are often three to nine people. And as always, the function matters, not the title.

2.title: The Four Agile Values
2.text: The Agile Manifesto names four values. Individuals and interactions over processes and tools. Working software over comprehensive documentation. Customer collaboration over contract negotiation. And responding to change over following a plan. The items on the right still have value. The items on the left are simply valued more. The wider principles include early and continuous delivery, welcoming change, daily work between business people and the team, sustainable pace, simplicity and self-organizing teams. This is exam practice, not PMBOK 8 text.

2.title: Roles in Adaptive Projects
2.text: Four groups of roles. The product owner maximizes the value of the product, owns and orders the backlog, speaks for the customer and accepts work. The scrum master, agile coach, or a project manager acting as servant leader, facilitates, removes impediments, coaches and shields the team. They do not assign tasks or micromanage. The team is cross-functional, self-organizing and ideally dedicated. It decides how to build, and commits to the iteration scope. And sponsors, customers and end users give direction, resources and feedback, mostly through the product owner.

2.title: Scrum at a Glance
2.text: Scrum is one widely used framework, and the exam may use its words. Three roles: product owner, scrum master and developers. One sprint, up to a month, contains four events: sprint planning, the daily scrum of fifteen minutes, the sprint review and the sprint retrospective. Three artifacts: the product backlog with its product goal, the sprint backlog with its sprint goal, and the increment, which meets the definition of done. PMBOK 8 uses neutral names: iteration, iteration planning, daily coordination meeting, review and retrospective.

2.title: Agile Planning Layers
2.text: Adaptive teams plan at five layers. The product vision says why the product exists. The product roadmap shows themes and direction over time. A release plan, typically three to six months, shows which features arrive in which release. An iteration plan fixes the committed scope for one to four weeks. And the daily plan is the daily coordination. Each layer is more detailed and shorter than the one above. Agile does not mean no planning. It means planning at several levels, and replanning often.

2.title: Backlogs
2.text: A backlog is an ordered list of work, often user stories, prioritized by the business. The product backlog holds all desired requirements, features, epics and stories. It represents the overall scope and vision. The release backlog is the subset planned for one release. The iteration backlog holds the stories and tasks selected for the current iteration. An epic is a large body of related work, split into stories. A user story describes an outcome from a stakeholder's view. Backlog management is how adaptive teams handle change, and refinement keeps upcoming work ready.

2.title: User Stories, Ready and Done
2.text: A user story states a role, a goal and a motivation, as in the example: a facilities manager wants a daily energy forecast to plan battery use. Acceptance criteria define the specific functionality and the user expectations to be met. The definition of ready, sometimes called a full kit, confirms that work is clear enough to start, which reduces rework. The definition of done is the checklist of everything a deliverable needs to be ready for customer use: testing, quality and compliance. Building these checks in each iteration is the shift-left idea.

2.title: Prioritizing the Backlog
2.text: Backlog items are ranked by business value or importance to the customer, sized by the team, with dependencies in mind. PMBOK 8 names four methods. MoSCoW sorts into must, should, could and will not have. The hundred-point method has stakeholders spend a hundred points across the items. Cost of delay asks what waiting costs. Kano analysis separates basic, performance and delighter features. Exam practice adds weighted shortest job first: cost of delay divided by job size, with the highest score going first. Small, urgent, valuable items rise.

2.title: Story Map and the MVP
2.text: A minimum viable product, the MVP, is the fewest features that deliver value, and it defines the first release. A story map helps check it. The backbone of user activities runs left to right. The details sit below each activity. Horizontal slices form releases. The first release must work end to end, like a walking skeleton. Scan the backbone column by column. If one column has nothing in release one, as pay does here, a customer cannot finish the journey, and the first release has a gap. A spike, a short investigation, can reduce a technical unknown first.

2.title: The Iteration Cycle
2.text: Each iteration repeats four events. Iteration planning: the team clarifies items, estimates effort and commits to a scope chosen from the prioritized backlog. Daily coordination: no more than fifteen minutes, covering what was done, what is planned and what blocks progress. Review: the team demonstrates completed work to stakeholders and asks for feedback, which shapes the backlog. Retrospective: the whole team explores what worked and what did not, to improve process and product. Backlog refinement runs alongside.

2.title: Iteration Events
2.text: Here is the same cycle as a table. Planning clarifies the items and criteria, and the team commits to scope from the prioritized backlog. Daily coordination lasts at most fifteen minutes and covers progress, plan and obstacles. It enables quick problem-solving, and it is for the team, not a status report to the project manager. The review demonstrates work and gathers feedback that shapes the backlog. The retrospective happens at least once per iteration, with actionable improvements and owners. Refinement is the ongoing preparation of upcoming work.

2.title: Reviews and Retrospectives That Work
2.text: Reviews and retrospectives often appear in exam scenarios. A review needs real discussion time, and the real customers or end users in the room, not only internal proxies. If feature completion is high but user ratings are falling, that is output without outcome. Do not wait weeks for feedback by email. A retrospective must change something. Pick a few improvements, give them owners and put them in the next backlog. If nothing changes after several retrospectives, inspect the improvement process itself.

2.title: Estimating and Velocity
2.text: Teams estimate in story points, a relative measure of effort. Comparing items is easier than predicting durations, so relative sizing is simpler without losing accuracy. PMBOK 8 names planning poker, story points and T-shirt sizing, among other techniques. Velocity is the rate at which deliverables are produced, validated and accepted within a predefined interval, and it helps forecast what a team can take on. It is team-specific. Do not compare teams or push it up. It measures output, not value, so also track outcomes and customer usage.

2.title: Burndown and Burnup Charts
2.text: Two charts show progress. A burndown chart shows work remaining against time left. The iteration burndown compares it with an ideal line, and a trend line forecasts completion. A burnup chart shows work completed toward a milestone, with total scope as a line across the top. When scope is added or removed, the scope line moves, so scope changes are visible. If scope grows, explain it with the burnup. Do not just pressure the team to go faster.

2.title: Cumulative Flow and Flow Measures
2.text: A cumulative flow diagram shows features completed over time, in each state, and in the backlog. A band that keeps widening marks a state where items arrive faster than they leave: the bottleneck. A flat done line means little is finishing. Know the flow measures. Throughput is items finished per period. Work in progress is items under way. Cycle time runs from starting a task to completing it. Lead time runs from the request to delivery. By Little's law, cycle time equals work in progress divided by throughput, so lower work in progress shortens cycle time. The flow measures and Little's law are exam practice, not PMBOK 8 formulas.

2.title: Kanban and WIP Limits
2.text: Kanban is a visual workflow method that limits work in process, drawing on lean principles. The board shows columns, and each active column has a limit. When a column nears its limit, the team swarms to help the work that is slowing the flow. Do not add work to a bottlenecked column. Kanban has no mandatory roles or iterations. Its principles are to visualize work, limit work in process, manage flow, make policies explicit, implement feedback loops and improve collaboratively.

2.title: Lean, Constraints and Visual Controls
2.text: Lean eliminates waste. Value stream mapping documents the steps and the time in a process, from customer request to value realized, so you can find the waste. The theory of constraints finds and addresses the biggest limiting factor. Visual controls and information radiators, such as task boards, burn charts and impediment lists, put progress where people actually look. Low tech, high touch is fine. Continuous improvement uses PDCA, Lean, total quality management and Six Sigma. And transparency means visible where stakeholders look.

2.title: Team Environment and Collaboration
2.text: The team environment matters. A team charter holds values, agreements and operating guidelines, and works best when the team develops it. Review it periodically, and revisit it with every new member. Colocation improves communication, while virtual collaboration tools support distributed teams. Dedicated, cross-functional members reduce context switching and waiting. Direct customer talks and testing build trust and quality. Design thinking, a human-centered, iterative process of understanding users, prototyping and testing, is popular for new products. If members breach their own charter, facilitate a team discussion.

2.title: Agile Across the Performance Domains
2.text: Here is how agile looks in each domain. Governance is lightweight, with periodic reviews and right-sized controls. Scope lives in a backlog that reflects current needs. Schedule uses release and iteration plans, timeboxes and burn charts. Finance allocates the budget quarterly and revises it quarterly, tracking spend per iteration. Stakeholders give continuous feedback in reviews, with information radiators. Resources are self-organizing, dedicated teams with servant leaders. Risk is reviewed each iteration in a risk-adjusted backlog. And quality sits in the definition of done.

2.title: Hybrid Ways of Working in Practice
2.text: Hybrid work needs clear practices. Choose per deliverable: stable, regulated, long-lead items predictive, uncertain items adaptive. Baseline the fixed elements, and use a roadmap and backlog for the rest. Report with a schedule executives recognize, with iteration detail beneath, and avoid turning a backlog into a false-precision Gantt chart. Use earned value or milestones for predictive streams, burn charts and velocity for agile ones, and one consolidated view for governance. Route routine backlog changes through the product owner, and baseline changes through formal control.

2.title: Predictive, Agile and Hybrid Compared
2.text: Put the three approaches side by side. Who manages: the project manager in predictive work, a self-organizing team with a product owner and a scrum master in agile work, and a shared arrangement in hybrid. Plans: a detailed baselined plan, versus a vision, roadmap, release and iteration plans, versus baselines plus a backlog. Change: formal change control, versus backlog reprioritization, versus a tailored mix. Progress: earned value and milestones, versus working increments, velocity and burn charts. The customer specifies up front in predictive work, and collaborates continuously in agile work.

2.title: Agile Traps: What PMI Expects
2.text: The traps for agile. Be a servant leader: facilitate and remove impediments. Do not assign tasks. The team commits to the iteration scope, so route new requests to the product owner and the backlog. The product owner owns priorities and value. Impediments get removed, not just logged. Retrospectives must change something. Velocity is output, not value. And agile does not mean no planning or no governance. When a senior stakeholder wants work added mid-iteration, represent the team's capacity and send the request to the product owner.

2.title: Part 2 Recap
2.text: Let us recap Part 2. Agile is a mindset broader than any framework, with servant leadership and function over title. Teams plan from vision to daily plan and keep ordered backlogs. Each iteration has planning, daily coordination, a review with real customers, and a retrospective that changes something. Velocity is output, the burnup shows scope, and the cumulative flow diagram shows bottlenecks. Flow uses work in process limits, swarming, lean and visual controls. And hybrid work chooses per deliverable, offers one reporting view and tailors change control. In Part 3, we turn to tailoring.

3.title: Tailoring: What It Is
3.text: Part 3 turns to tailoring. Tailoring is the deliberate adaptation of the approach, governance and processes to fit the project's environment and objectives. It is driven by the principles, and by organizational values and culture. A low risk appetite tends to mean structured processes and oversight, while a higher tolerance may favor agility. Tailoring means mindfully selecting and adjusting what is useful. Projects balance competing demands. And policy or a contract may mandate an approach and limit tailoring. Tailor within policy, justify the change and check that it works.

3.title: Why Tailor
3.text: Why tailor? There is no single approach for all projects. Structures range from extensive to minimal, and from rigorous to lightweight. Variables include criticality, scale, duration and complexity. They include industry standards and organizational culture. And they include the number of stakeholders and the maturity of project management. A nuclear reactor project needs far more rigor than an office building, and a ten-person team needs far less coordination than a two-hundred-person team. Too few processes make management ineffective, and too many are costly. Teams that help tailor are more committed.

3.title: What You Can Tailor
3.text: You can tailor three things. First, the life cycle and development approach: the phases, and predictive, adaptive or hybrid. A data center with predictive construction and an adaptive approach for computing capabilities is a hybrid at project level, though each sub-team experiences only one approach. Second, the processes. Third, engagement. That covers the people, meaning the skills of leaders and team. It covers empowerment, meaning which decisions are delegated. And it covers integration, meaning making one team from contractors, partners and staff.

3.title: Five Ways to Tailor a Process
3.text: You can tailor a process in five ways. Add: for unique conditions or more rigor. Modify: adjust inputs, outputs, tools and techniques to fit your needs. Remove: cut unnecessary cost or effort. Blend: combine elements for added value. Align: give a consistent definition and application across the organization. Too few processes make management ineffective. More than required is wasteful. But do not unilaterally drop required steps. If a policy or contract requires them, request an approved exception.

3.title: The Tailoring Process
3.text: Tailoring follows four steps. One: select the initial development approach. Two: tailor for the organization, within policy and PMO guidance. Three: tailor for the project, looking at the product, the team and the culture. Four: implement ongoing improvement. It is not a one-time exercise. Issues with how the team works, or how the product evolves, signal further tailoring. Review points, phase gates and retrospectives are chances to inspect and adapt. Rigid persistence with a failing approach is wrong.

3.title: Step 1: Select the Initial Approach
3.text: Step one: select the initial development approach. Use product knowledge, the delivery cadence and your awareness of the options. A suitability filter is a decision-making aid that assesses culture, team dynamics and project factors to guide the choice among predictive, adaptive and hybrid. It is not a rigid method, and you combine it with other data, such as requirements stability and regulation. The filter helps you decide. It does not decide for you.

3.title: Step 2: Tailor for the Organization
3.text: Step two: tailor for the organization. Teams own and improve their processes, but organizations provide methodologies as starting points for repeatable processes and consistent measurement. With process governance, you align tailoring with policy. Consider the program and portfolio context, because aligning tailoring across related projects improves consistency. A PMO often reviews and approves tailored approaches. Tailoring that affects only the project team usually needs just the project manager's approval. Tailoring that affects external groups may need PMO approval. In multi-organization projects, tailor jointly.

3.title: Step 3: Tailor for the Project
3.text: Step three: tailor for the project, asking questions about three attributes. The product or deliverable: how much rigor do standards require? Is it a well-known product or intangible? Is the market regulated or fast moving? Is the technology stable? How stable are the requirements, and can it be delivered incrementally? The project team: size, geography, experience, access to the customer, and diversity of skills. And culture: buy-in to the approach, trust that the team will deliver, empowerment, and how decisions are made.

3.title: Step 4: Keep Improving
3.text: Step four: keep improving. Tailoring is not a one-time exercise. When the team struggles with how it works, or the product evolves, that signals more tailoring. Review points, phase gates and retrospectives are the moments to inspect and adapt the process, the development approach and the delivery frequency. Keeping the team engaged in improving its own process builds pride of ownership, and shows trust. Even the way an organization tailors can itself be tailored. Do not impose a process change without the team's input.

3.title: Diagnostics: Quality, Team and Approvals
3.text: Diagnostics link a situation to a tailoring suggestion. Poor quality: find the root causes and improve the process, rather than only adding more verification. Team members unsure how to proceed: assess their needs, and offer guidance, mentoring, training and knowledge sharing. Members who are uncooperative and work in silos: team building and individual conversations to find the cause. Long delays waiting for approvals: streamline by appointing people who are authorized to decide up to value thresholds. Fix the cause, not the symptom.

3.title: Diagnostics: Flow, Stakeholders, Transparency and Risk
3.text: More diagnostics. Too much work in progress and waste: use value stream mapping and Kanban boards to visualize the work and find fixes. Stakeholders who are disengaged or negative: check they receive timely, relevant information, and tailor the communication methods. No transparency about progress: make sure the right data is collected, analyzed, shared and discussed, and that everyone agrees on the measures. Issues and risks that keep surfacing unprepared: explore root causes, and look for gaps in processes or activities. Periodic reviews show whether the approach works.

3.title: Case Check-In: Tailoring the Microgrid
3.text: Let us tailor the microgrid. In the build lane, the team keeps phase gates, formal change control and detailed baselines. In the software lane, a product owner orders the backlog, iterations last two weeks, and retrospectives tune the process. The bridge between them needs tailoring. The steering committee gets one reporting view. Backlog changes go through the product owner, while baseline changes go through the change control board. Because the reporting affects outside groups, the PMO must approve it.

3.title: Tailoring in Predictive, Agile and Hybrid Work
3.text: Tailoring differs by approach. In predictive work, you tailor planning detail, gates, control rigor and reporting. The project manager owns it, with the PMO, within policy, triggered by size, criticality and regulation. In agile work, you tailor iteration length, events, the definition of done and board design. The team owns it through retrospectives. In hybrid work, you tailor which streams use which approach, the interfaces and one reporting view. Poor tailoring costs something in each approach: bureaucracy, ritual without value, or mixed signals.

3.title: Tailoring Traps: What PMI Expects
3.text: The traps for tailoring. Tailor. Do not blindly apply the standard or discard it. Contracts and policies limit tailoring, so work within them or request an exception. Fix the cause, not the symptom: poor quality calls for root cause and process improvement, slow approvals call for delegated authority thresholds, and silos call for team building. Tailoring is continuous. Involve the team. And use the PMO when the change affects others. Document the reasoning for every tailoring decision.

3.title: Module Recap
3.text: Let us recap the whole module. Match predictive, adaptive or hybrid to the context. Gates decide, and the cost of change rises over time in predictive work. In agile work, practice servant leadership, keep ordered backlogs, protect the iteration, manage flow and use honest measures. In hybrid work, choose per deliverable, offer one reporting view and tailor change control. Tailoring has four steps and five ways, stays within policy, and never stops. Now it is time to test yourself. Five questions follow. For each one, pause the video, choose your answer, and then listen to the explanation.

3.title: Practice Question 1
3.text: Question one. A university is building a research laboratory with fixed design drawings and permits, and a visitor tracking app whose features are still unclear to the stakeholders. Which approach should the project manager recommend? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is A. The scenario mixes a stable, permitted build with an uncertain software feature set, so a hybrid lets each deliverable follow the approach that suits it. One approach for both ignores the difference, and switching the whole project later does not fit work that runs in parallel.

3.title: Practice Question 2
3.text: Question two. A phase review finds that two of the five exit criteria are unmet, yet the contractors for the next phase are already mobilizing. What should the project manager do? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is D. A gate is a decision point. With unmet criteria, the options include continuing with modification, repeating the phase or parts of it, remaining in it, or ending it. The authority decides on the facts. Pushing ahead, misreporting, or cancelling outright skips that decision.

3.title: Practice Question 3
3.text: Question three. An agile team has a fixed budget and a fixed end date, and new high-priority requests keep arriving. How should the project manager handle this? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is B. When budget and schedule are fixed, scope is the variable, so the product owner reorders the backlog by value and the lowest-value items drop out. Extending the limits, overtime, or blanket refusal ignores the constraint or the value.

3.title: Practice Question 4
3.text: Question four. Halfway through an iteration, a senior executive asks the project manager to add an urgent feature to the team's work. The team has committed to its iteration scope. What should the project manager do? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is C. The team's commitment inside an iteration is protected, and new requests go to the product owner, who decides the order of the backlog by value. Adding work, refusing outright, or leaving the choice to the team misreads who owns priorities.

3.title: Practice Question 5
3.text: Question five. A project's work stalls because every purchase and design decision waits weeks for a single senior approver. Which tailoring suggestion fits best? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is A. Delays in approvals are a tailoring signal: streamline by delegating authority to decide up to value thresholds, which keeps control while removing the bottleneck. Pressure fixes the symptom, removing approvals drops needed control, and extra reviews add delay.

3.title: Answers at a Glance
3.text: Here are all five answers together. Question one: A. A stable build and an uncertain app call for a hybrid. Question two: D. A gate is a decision point for the authority. Question three: B. With budget and date fixed, scope flexes. Question four: C. New requests go to the product owner, not into the iteration. Question five: A. Delegate approval authority up to value thresholds. That completes Module 2. Next, Module 3 covers the PMI Code of Ethics, sustainability and artificial intelligence. See you there.
